newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Patria sees Czech 1996 c/a deficit at 7 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Patria sees Czech 1996 c/a deficit at 7 pct of GDP.

text.p: Prague-based Patria Finance said on Wednesday that a widening of the Czech trade deficit could force the 1996 current account deficit to rise to seven percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from four percent in 1995.
It forecast the current account deficit could rise to eight percent of GDP in 1997.
Patria said it also expected a "marked slowdown" in foreign capital inflow to a net inflow totalling $3 billion in 1996 down from $8.23 billion last year, and remaining flat in 1997.

"Less political stability, concerns about the current account and a perceived lack of transparency of Czech capital markets will contribute to lacklustre capital inflow," Patria economists said in a research report to investors.
"Negligible foreign indebtedness, huge foreign exchange reserves, and balanced fiscal accounts, on the other hand, will work against the slowdown," it added.
The eight-month trade deficit stood at 100 billion crowns surpassing the total for the whole of 1995.

Patria said a substantial part of the imports, which it forecast to grow by about 15.5 percent this year and 15 percent next year, "represent purchases of machinery and technology that could help reverse the trade balance deterioration."
Meanwhile it said exports were expected to grow by 7.5 percent in 1996 and accelerate to 12 percent growth in 1997.

But Patria said that it fears negative economic news such as the worsening trade deficit and state budget battles "might provoke a chain reaction" with destabilising consequences for the overall economy.

"Given the long lags between economic policy implementation and its impact on the economy, we believe, that now is the time to take serious action to prevent this macroeconomic imbalance from becoming, unmanagable," the report said.

Patria advocates that the government pass a surplus budget for 1997 of 1-3 percent of GDP -- instead of its fifth balanced budget -- along with policies to promote domestic savings in order to slow domestic demand.
"A budget surplus is the best solution for the growing disparity between domestic savings and investments in the short run," it said.
